misconceptions.believed: The test suite failing on this machine meant a regression in the repository that had to be fixed before any new work started.
misconceptions.revealed_by: Six failures, all op-count comparisons, all reporting fewer operations than the baseline (1364 against 2184 for w1-l3-join). A regression that makes the reference solution do less work while still passing is not a plausible bug. The baseline records python_version 3.11.15; the machine runs 3.14.7.
misconceptions.corrected_to: Op counts are a property of the interpreter as much as of the code. CPython changed how the constructs in those two levels compile between 3.11 and 3.14. Installing 3.11.15 turned the suite green with no source change.
misconceptions.generalisable_lesson: The rule that says stop on a red baseline is what distinguished an environment mismatch from a regression; had the work started first, the six failures would have been attributed to the new module. A measurement that encodes its own environment (python_version in the baseline file) is what made the diagnosis take minutes instead of an afternoon.

misconceptions.believed: A backend availability probe can ask `docker version --format '{{.Server.Version}}'` and trust a zero exit status.
misconceptions.revealed_by: The probe reported Docker available while /var/run/docker.sock did not exist. The command exits 0 and prints a version regardless, because the client answers for the server when the server is absent.
misconceptions.corrected_to: `docker info --format '{{.ServerVersion}}'`, which prints an empty string when the daemon is unreachable, plus a _probe_ok hook so a backend can demand more than an exit status.
misconceptions.generalisable_lesson: A CLI that wraps a daemon will often answer questions about itself when the daemon is gone. Probe for a value only the daemon can supply, and check the value rather than the exit status.

decisions.decision: Bubblewrap is the primary isolating backend; Docker is the fallback
alternatives: Docker only, as T2 W1 words it
decisions.rationale: 8.8x less overhead for the same isolation properties, no daemon and no root required. The trajectory says container-backed; its exit criteria describe isolation properties, and those are what got built.

decisions.decision: A backend contributes argv and nothing else
alternatives: Backends own the whole run and parse cycle
decisions.rationale: A transport that can shape the result is a transport that can change a score.

decisions.decision: An unavailable pinned backend raises instead of falling back
alternatives: Warn and downgrade to the subprocess path
decisions.rationale: A silent downgrade to the host process is the exact failure the module exists to prevent, and it surfaces as an incident rather than a test failure.

decisions.decision: One cold container per Docker run, no warm pool
decisions.rationale: The trajectory's own hazard note: pools are the standard source of state leaks between runs, and here a leak means one player's code seeing another's.

decisions.decision: untrusted is a run_code keyword defaulting to False
decisions.rationale: Keeps one code path under test, and makes W3 a one-line change at each call site rather than a re-architecture.

friction.description: The Docker daemon was inactive and disabled at session start, and starting it requires a password the session does not have. It became active partway through, which is the only reason DockerBackend could be verified rather than merely written.

Finding the minimal bubblewrap bind set took several probe cycles. Binding / read-only works immediately and is wrong: it satisfies read-only rootfs while leaving exit criterion 2 failing, since the whole host stays readable. The narrow set had to be found empirically because the interpreter's shared-library dependencies are distribution-specific.

The system interpreter is 3.14.7 and cannot run the suite green. Every command this session ran under uv-provided 3.11.15, which is friction every future session on this machine inherits until Q11 is settled.

open_questions.question: Op counts are interpreter-version-bound (M5). Should the project pin an interpreter, record a per-version baseline, or compare within a tolerance? A pin contradicts 'runs anywhere a Python 3.10+ interpreter does'; a tolerance weakens the guard that caught M5.
The Docker image is pinned by tag (python:3.11-slim), which is mutable. Pin by digest, or accept the drift given that the harness is stdlib-only?
Bubblewrap's bind set is derived from sys.base_prefix at call time. Does that hold for a frozen or statically linked interpreter, or must the backend declare itself unavailable there?
